slice_results.behavior_summary: When called, the code reads a CSV file from a user-supplied or command-line specified filepath using fs and csv-parse, processes the data with a concave hull calculation, then writes the processed output to a specified or default file path using fs.writeFile, enabling file read and write operations based on external input. No hardcoded IPs, URLs, shell commands, or encoded strings are present, and no network or system execution APIs are invoked, resulting in standard file processing without evident security risks.
slice_results.explanation: [LLM Judgment: Benign] The analyzed code performs standard file input/output operations and data processing using well-known Node.js modules (fs, csv-parse, csv-stringify) and a local module for concave hull calculation. It reads a CSV file specified by the user, processes the data, and writes the output to a file. There are no indications of network communication, data exfiltration, system command execution, or access to sensitive information. Compared to the known malicious patterns, this code lacks any suspicious API usage such as child_process execution, network requests, or harvesting of sensitive data. The behavior is consistent with legitimate data processing scripts.

matched_snippet.code_behavior: Upon manual execution, the code collects the current user's username, hostname, and public IP address using os and child_process modules, then sends this data via HTTPS POST to hits.dwyl.com, providing an alternate exfiltration channel for host information to an attacker-controlled domain.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: The code is functionally identical to the malicious preinstall script but targets a different exfiltration endpoint. Its presence in index.js, the main entry point of the package, suggests intent to provide a backup or alternate channel for data exfiltration, even if the preinstall script is blocked or removed.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Legitimate index.js files in npm packages are expected to provide the main library functionality, not to collect and transmit sensitive host information or make unsolicited network requests.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: There are no legitimate use cases for index.js to silently collect and exfiltrate host information. Standard practice is to only collect anonymized telemetry with user consent and clear documentation.
key_indicators: Collection of sensitive host information (username, hostname, public IP) in index.js
Outbound HTTPS POST request to hits.dwyl.com, a non-standard and attacker-controlled endpoint
Redundant exfiltration logic mirroring the preinstall script
No user notification, consent, or documentation of data collection
Use of os, https, and child_process modules for data collection and transmission

package_info.why_malicious: The package is malicious because it surreptitiously collects sensitive host information (username, hostname, and public IP address) during installation and exfiltrates it to attacker-controlled endpoints without user knowledge or consent. It was distributed as part of a large-scale typosquatting campaign, mimicking popular libraries to deceive users and facilitate unauthorized data collection.

attack_chain.action: User installs the malicious npm package (e.g., angulerjs@1.1.3).
The preinstall script (new.js) is executed, collecting username, hostname, and public IP address from the host system.
Collected data is sent via HTTPS POST to a Discord webhook controlled by the attacker.
If index.js is executed (manually or by other means), it collects the same information and sends it to hits.dwyl.com.
attack_chain.leads_to: Provides an alternate exfiltration channel for the attacker.

behavioral_signatures: npm preinstall scripts that collect and exfiltrate system information (username, hostname, public IP) during installation
Outbound network requests to Discord webhooks or suspicious domains (e.g., hits.dwyl.com) from installation scripts
Presence of redundant exfiltration logic in both preinstall scripts and main entry points (e.g., new.js and index.js)
file_indicators: package.json with preinstall field referencing suspicious scripts such as new.js
new.js or index.js files containing combined use of os, https, and child_process modules for data collection and transmission
Hardcoded references to external domains such as discord.com/api/webhooks or hits.dwyl.com in JavaScript files
network_indicators: Outbound HTTPS POST requests to hits.dwyl.com/api/collect
detection_knowledge.how_to_detect: Monitor npm package installations for preinstall scripts that access system information (username, hostname, public IP) and initiate outbound network requests to external domains, especially Discord webhooks or non-standard endpoints like hits.dwyl.com. Flag packages with suspiciously named scripts (e.g., new.js) referenced in package.json preinstall fields. Use static analysis to detect the use of os, https, and child_process modules in installation or entry-point scripts, and employ network monitoring to identify exfiltration attempts to known malicious endpoints. Pay special attention to packages with names mimicking popular libraries, as these are common in typosquatting campaigns.

matched_knowledge.source_package: TeamViewer.exe / BetterShaders Setup 1.0.3.exe / Software.exe (malicious Electron apps) (NSIS installer (Electron app distribution))

matched_snippet.code_behavior: At runtime (upon application execution), the code collects system information, browser history, and credentials from the filesystem using Node.js APIs, then sends this data via an outbound HTTP POST request to the gofile.io file-sharing service, resulting in exfiltration of sensitive user data to an external attacker.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: The code programmatically accesses sensitive files such as browser history and credential stores, then transmits this data to an external file-sharing service (gofile.io) without user knowledge or consent. This behavior is characteristic of infostealer malware.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Legitimate Electron applications should not access or transmit user credentials, browser history, or detailed system information without explicit user consent and clear disclosure. Accessing and exfiltrating such data is a direct violation of user privacy and security expectations.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: Some legitimate applications may collect anonymized telemetry or crash logs, but they do not access credential stores or browser histories, and always request user consent for any data collection or transmission.
key_indicators: Direct file access to browser history and credential files from within Electron app resources
Outbound HTTP POST requests to gofile.io/upload or similar file-sharing endpoints
Node.js code embedded in .asar archives performing OS-level data harvesting
Absence of user prompts or consent dialogs for sensitive data access or transmission

required_permissions: filesystem (read access to browser and credential files)

package_info.package_name: TeamViewer.exe / BetterShaders Setup 1.0.3.exe / Software.exe (malicious Electron apps)
package_info.why_malicious: These packages are Electron-based desktop applications distributed via NSIS installers that contain malicious Node.js code within their .asar archives. The code is designed to harvest sensitive user data, including system information, browser histories, and credentials, and exfiltrate it to external file-sharing services such as gofile.io. The applications masquerade as legitimate software to evade detection and facilitate data theft.

attack_chain.action: User downloads and executes a trojanized Electron app distributed as an NSIS installer.
attack_chain.leads_to: Malicious Electron app is installed and launched.

attack_chain.action: Electron app unpacks and executes Node.js code from the .asar archive (a.js) upon application startup.
attack_chain.leads_to: Malicious code is loaded into memory and prepared for execution.

attack_chain.action: Malicious Node.js code collects system information, browser history, and credentials from the victim's machine.
attack_chain.leads_to: Sensitive data is gathered from the victim's machine.

attack_chain.action: Collected data is exfiltrated to gofile.io via HTTP POST request.
attack_chain.leads_to: Attacker receives stolen data via the file-sharing service.

behavioral_signatures: Electron app accessing browser history and credential files without user consent
Electron app making outbound HTTP POST requests to file-sharing services such as gofile.io
Node.js code within .asar archives performing OS-level data collection and exfiltration
file_indicators: Presence of suspicious .asar files in Electron app resources (e.g., app\resources\app.asar\a.js)
NSIS installer files with hashes: 9926e2782d603061b52d88f83d93e7af, cfc6e0014b3cc8d4dcaf0d76e2382556, b150afa6b3642ea1da1233b76f7b454e
network_indicators: Outbound connections to https://gofile.io/upload from Electron app processes
Unusual HTTP POST requests containing system or credential data to file-sharing domains
detection_knowledge.how_to_detect: Monitor Electron-based applications for unauthorized access to sensitive files such as browser history and credential stores. Inspect .asar archives for embedded Node.js scripts that perform data harvesting or exfiltration. Flag NSIS installers with known malicious hashes or those that unpack Electron apps exhibiting these behaviors. Monitor network traffic for outbound HTTP POST requests to gofile.io/upload or similar file-sharing services originating from Electron app processes.

matched_knowledge.source_package: various (over 1200) CuteBoi-related packages (names randomized, e.g., cloudyboi12, etc.) (npm)

matched_snippet.code_behavior: At runtime, the code executes a bundled XMRig binary using Node.js child_process.execFile, passing a configuration file as an argument, which causes the host system to initiate unauthorized cryptocurrency mining and send results to attacker-controlled endpoints.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: The code launches a bundled cryptocurrency miner (XMRig) without user knowledge or consent, using a configuration that benefits the attacker. This is a hallmark of cryptojacking malware.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Legitimate npm packages should not execute hidden mining binaries or initiate resource-intensive processes that connect to external mining pools without explicit user consent and transparency.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: Legitimate mining utilities may execute mining binaries, but only after explicit user action and with user-supplied configuration, not silently or with attacker-controlled settings.
key_indicators: Automatic execution of a bundled XMRig binary at runtime
Use of child_process.execFile to launch external binaries
Configuration file path hardcoded to attacker-supplied config
No user interaction or consent required for mining to begin

execution_context.trigger: runtime (when the package is imported and its main function is invoked by another program)
execution_context.file_location: main JavaScript file (e.g., index.js) within the package root directory

package_info.package_name: various (over 1200) CuteBoi-related packages (names randomized, e.g., cloudyboi12, etc.)
package_info.package_versions: all published versions (over 1200 packages, each with initial version)
package_info.why_malicious: These packages are direct clones of the eazyminer package, each embedding XMRig cryptocurrency mining binaries and configuration files that direct mined currency to attacker-controlled endpoints. The packages are distributed at scale via automated, disposable npm accounts, indicating a coordinated, large-scale cryptojacking campaign. The presence of mining binaries and attacker-controlled wallet configuration is not expected in legitimate npm packages, and the packages are designed to exploit unsuspecting users' compute resources for illicit profit.

attack_chain.action: Attacker publishes over 1200 npm packages, each embedding a miner binary and attacker-controlled configuration file.
attack_chain.leads_to: Packages are available for installation by unsuspecting users.

attack_chain.action: User or automated system (e.g., CI/CD pipeline) installs and imports the malicious package.
attack_chain.leads_to: Malicious code and binaries are present on the host system and ready for execution.

attack_chain.action: When invoked, the package's JavaScript code launches the XMRig miner binary with the attacker-supplied configuration.
attack_chain.leads_to: Host system begins mining Monero for the attacker's benefit, consuming CPU and network resources.

attack_chain.action: Mined cryptocurrency is sent to attacker-controlled wallet via attacker-controlled mining pool endpoint.
attack_chain.leads_to: Attacker profits from unauthorized use of victim's compute resources.

behavioral_signatures: npm packages that contain and execute XMRig or other cryptocurrency mining binaries at runtime
Automatic execution of bundled binaries via child_process or similar APIs
Presence of hardcoded mining pool URLs and wallet addresses in configuration files
Mining activity initiated without user interaction or consent
file_indicators: Presence of XMRig binaries (Windows/Linux) with randomized or misleading names in package directories
config.json or similarly named files containing mining pool configuration with attacker-controlled endpoints
Unusual binary files present in npm package root or subdirectories unrelated to stated package functionality
network_indicators: Outbound connections to known mining pools or attacker-controlled endpoints (e.g., knowledgemd[.]com, scpulse[.]com, idots[.]cf, fisch[.]ml, Nordalts[.]ml, 130.162.52[.]80)
Network traffic to domains or IPs not associated with legitimate mining pools, especially those hardcoded in package configuration
detection_knowledge.how_to_detect: Scan npm packages for embedded mining binaries such as XMRig, especially those with randomized or misleading names. Analyze configuration files for hardcoded mining pool URLs and wallet addresses that do not belong to the user. Monitor for unexpected process execution of mining binaries and outbound network connections to known mining pool domains or suspicious IP addresses. Flag packages that include binaries unrelated to their stated functionality or that match known cryptominer hashes. Correlate file, process, and network indicators to identify automated cryptojacking campaigns.

matched_snippet.code_behavior: At runtime, shortly after import, the code initiates a delayed execution using setTimeout, performs an external geolocation API request, parses the response to determine the user's country, and if the country is Russia or Belarus, recursively calls a file deletion function on multiple directory levels, resulting in destructive file overwrites.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: The code makes an unsolicited external geolocation API request and, based on the result, triggers recursive file overwrite operations targeting the entire filesystem. This is a clear indicator of a targeted, destructive payload.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: A legitimate IPC package should not perform geolocation checks or attempt to overwrite user files under any circumstances. The expected behavior is to provide inter-process communication utilities, not to execute destructive actions based on user location.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: Geolocation checks may be used for regional feature toggling or compliance, but never to trigger destructive file operations. Recursive file deletion is only appropriate in uninstallers or cleanup tools, and only with explicit user consent.
key_indicators: Automated geolocation API request at runtime
Conditional logic targeting specific countries (Russia, Belarus)
Recursive invocation of file overwrite function across multiple directory levels
Destructive file operations triggered without user interaction

package_info.why_malicious: The package was intentionally altered by its maintainer to include code that, upon execution, checks the user's geolocation via an external API. If the user is located in Russia or Belarus, the code recursively overwrites files across the filesystem with a heart emoji, resulting in widespread and deliberate data destruction. This constitutes a targeted sabotage attack, which is entirely outside the scope of legitimate package behavior.

attack_chain.action: On package installation or import, the malicious code in dao/ssl-geospec.js is loaded and scheduled for execution via setTimeout.
attack_chain.leads_to: Geolocation check and potential execution of destructive payload

attack_chain.action: The code performs an external geolocation API request to determine if the user is located in Russia or Belarus.
attack_chain.leads_to: Conditional execution of recursive file overwrite function

attack_chain.action: If the user is in a targeted country, the code recursively attempts to overwrite all files on the system with a heart emoji.
attack_chain.leads_to: Destruction of user and system data

attack_chain.action: In related packages (peacenotwar, oneday-test), the code writes a protest message file to user Desktop and OneDrive directories.
attack_chain.leads_to: Display of unsolicited political/protest message in user-accessible locations

behavioral_signatures: JavaScript packages that make runtime geolocation API requests and subsequently perform recursive filesystem operations or file overwrites
Recursive file overwrite attempts targeting user and system directories, especially with static content (e.g., heart emoji)
Creation of unsolicited files with political or protest content in user Desktop or OneDrive directories
detection_knowledge.how_to_detect: Monitor for JavaScript packages that initiate external geolocation API requests at runtime, especially if followed by recursive filesystem operations or file overwrites. Flag any package that writes unsolicited files to user Desktop or OneDrive directories, or that contains the file dao/ssl-geospec.js. Alert on the presence of WITH-LOVE-FROM-AMERICA.txt in user directories. Correlate destructive file operations or unusual file creation with recent package updates or new dependencies to identify malicious activity.

matched_snippet.code_behavior: At runtime, index.js collects the current OS username and working directory, transmits this information to a remote attacker-controlled server via HTTP GET, recursively searches the filesystem for sensitive files and directories (such as .env, .gitlab, .github, and files with extensions like .asp, .js, .php), archives the discovered files into a ZIP archive, and uploads the archive to a predefined external FTP server, resulting in exfiltration of sensitive developer data.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: Automated collection and exfiltration of user and file data to external servers is a hallmark of infostealer malware, especially when targeting developer secrets and project files.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Legitimate packages do not search for, archive, or exfiltrate user files or environment information without explicit user consent and to trusted destinations.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: Backup or deployment tools may archive and upload files, but only with user consent and to trusted, user-configured destinations—not to hardcoded, attacker-controlled infrastructure.
key_indicators: collecting OS username and working directory without user interaction
HTTP requests to hardcoded, attacker-controlled domains
recursive search for sensitive files and directories
creation of ZIP archives containing project or configuration files
FTP upload of archives to external, untrusted servers

execution_context.trigger: runtime (immediately after install, via detached process)

package_info.why_malicious: CryptoRocket is malicious because it is engineered to automatically execute code upon installation that exfiltrates sensitive data—including source code, configuration files, and environment information—from the developer's machine to attacker-controlled infrastructure. The package structure (package.json, preinstall.js, index.js) is intentionally orchestrated to enable stealthy data theft and unauthorized remote communication, with no legitimate functionality.

attack_chain.action: Malicious package is installed, triggering the postinstall script in package.json.
preinstall.js spawns index.js as a detached background process to persist after installation.
attack_chain.leads_to: index.js runs independently in the background

attack_chain.action: index.js collects user and environment data, recursively searches for sensitive files, archives them, and exfiltrates the data to attacker-controlled infrastructure via HTTP and FTP.
attack_chain.leads_to: Data exfiltration and compromise of developer secrets

behavioral_signatures: npm package with postinstall script executing a custom JavaScript file (e.g., preinstall.js)
installation-time spawning of detached background processes using child_process.spawn with detached: true
runtime file system enumeration and archiving of sensitive files or directories
network connections to hardcoded, untrusted external servers via HTTP or FTP
creation and FTP upload of ZIP archives containing project or configuration files immediately after installation
file_indicators: package.json with a postinstall script referencing preinstall.js
presence of both preinstall.js and index.js in the package root directory
creation of ZIP archives containing source code or configuration files in the user's project directory
network_indicators: HTTP GET requests to attacker-controlled domains/IPs (see IOC list)
FTP connections to unknown external servers for file uploads
Domains: oastify.com, requestbin.net, canarytokens.com, oast.fun, pipedream.net, nirobtest.xyz, marcomayo.com, npmtesttut.com
detection_knowledge.how_to_detect: Monitor npm package installations for postinstall scripts that launch custom JavaScript files, especially those that spawn detached background processes. Flag packages containing both preinstall.js and index.js with logic for file system enumeration and network exfiltration. Detect outbound HTTP or FTP connections to known malicious domains or IPs, and alert on ZIP archive creation containing sensitive project files immediately after package installation. Correlate these behaviors to identify coordinated data exfiltration attempts.
